records.targetRef: Likkutei Maamarim, On Book of Joshua 10
records.themeTitle: The leader and the generation’s combined soul
records.themeSummary: A generation’s many spiritual powers are described as gathered in its leader.
records.explanation: Likkutei Maamarim explains the siman's statement that the generation's thoughts and desires build the stature of its leader. Their gathering is itself described as a distinct soul, with the leader including their wisdom and powers. This makes the relation reciprocal rather than a claim about popularity, and clarifies why the siman discusses the generation's brief illumination and its leader together.
records.targetEnglish: It is known that the leader of a generation has a soul encompassing all the souls of that generation, as the Sages said (Arakhin 17a), a leader according to the generation, and a generation according to the leader. Every generation is a particular arrangement of the souls of that generation—that is, parts of Hashem's wisdom, as explained. The gathering of all those wisdoms is itself also one soul. Souls divide into details and further details according to the order Hashem arranged, and their totality is itself a distinct soul, different from the details taken alone. The father's soul includes the souls of all his children; Adam included the souls of all the generations, and their totality was Adam's distinct soul. Likewise, the leader's soul includes all the generation's souls, as a king is the whole nation. He can therefore lead them all, because his wisdom includes all their wisdom, and likewise his understanding and all his spiritual powers.

records.themeTitle: Faith that does not force the time
records.themeSummary: Hope in a spiritual rescue can be patient while the path remains hidden.
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim explains the same ‘trust in Hashem’ passage through a definition of faith: holding to what has not yet become clear without forcing its time. This qualifies the siman's permission to hope for an unexpected spiritual rescue. The hope accompanies its stated first response of doing good and prayer; it is not a timetable imposed on the rescue.
records.targetEnglish: Emunah is related to ‘as a nurse carries the infant.’ As the Tikkunei Zohar explains (introduction, 2a), ‘the father of faith, which is understanding.’ One should not hasten the time or press the hour, but wait in faith. Then this kindness will be revealed, and he will recognize it within his understanding too. ‘Tend faith’ means to guard the matter until it is also revealed in one's understanding. The term faith applies only to what is not explicit in one's understanding: what is already explicit needs no faith. What is not explicit requires faith—guarding the matter well until it emerges into explicit revelation before human eyes.

records.themeTitle: Prayer that reawakens Torah acquired through effort
records.themeSummary: The loss of felt illumination need not erase what labor has established in the heart.
records.explanation: Tiferet Yosef adds a distinction to the siman's account of first light and prayer. A gift can be lost when attention moves away; Torah acquired through effort becomes fixed enough to be awakened again through prayer. This explains a way in which the plea to preserve the first desire works together with the learner's subsequent labor.
records.targetEnglish: When Hashem gives a person illumination of understanding in the light of Torah, without the person having endured or labored for those words of Torah, then if he turns his attention away even for a moment, Scripture says (Proverbs 23:5), ‘Will you set your eyes upon it? It is gone.’ As the Jerusalem Talmud says at the end of Berakhot in the name of the Scroll of the Pious: if you leave it one day, it leaves you two. But Torah that comes through labor, for which the person has endured, becomes fixed in his heart and will not let him turn away. As it says (Deuteronomy 32:2), ‘May my teaching drop like rain’: my holy grandfather explained that Torah for which a person labors holds him from behind his neck and will not let him turn away, like someone holding his fellow so he cannot leave. If the person nevertheless turns away from Torah that came through labor, he can reawaken it through much prayer and regain his former illumination. Through the endurance and labor he devoted to it, it became fixed in his heart, and he can reawaken the Torah repeatedly through prayer.

records.themeTitle: The thought that holds the heart’s life
records.themeSummary: A central attachment is distinguished from the outer passing garments of thought.
records.explanation: Machshavot Charutz makes an explicit distinction relevant to ‘where his thought is attached.’ The thought carrying the heart's central life defines the person at depth; other thoughts can be outer garments. It also acknowledges how difficult it is to be entirely free of a momentary other thought. This helps read the siman's language of attachment with precision while preserving the task of directing thought toward Torah.
records.targetEnglish: A thought of this kind, upon which the heart's principal point of life depends, is the essence of the person—not the other outer thoughts, which are garments of the inward and principal thought. Almost no person is completely pure even in thought's outer garment, belonging to Hashem alone so that no other thought rises in his mind for even one moment throughout his life.
records.originHebrew: וּמָקוֹם שֶׁמַּחֲשַׁבְתּוֹ אֲדוּקָה, כָּךְ הוּא כָּל צוּרַת הָאָדָם בְּאוֹתוֹ עֵת.
records.originEnglish: And where his thought is bound fast, such is the entire form of the person at that moment.

records.themeTitle: The mitzvah itself as the future delight
records.themeSummary: The good tasted after labor is described as a deeper enjoyment of the service itself.
records.explanation: Peri Tzadik explains the continuity between a person's embodied service and the good tasted afterward. Torah and the mitzvah meal become the very forms of future delight, rather than a reward detached from the service. This develops the siman's final distinction between the deed alone and enjoyment that makes its inward life perceptible.
records.targetEnglish: It is known that the reward of a mitzvah is the mitzvah itself: one merits that very matter. Thus Torah scholars have no rest in the world to come, as it says, ‘They go from strength to strength’ (Berakhot 64a). Through their engagement in Torah in this world, they merit delighting in Torah in the world to come. Likewise, through the mitzvah meal they observe in this world, they merit the feast of the righteous in the future, which is the culmination of holy delight, as explained in the holy books. As the Sages said: through fulfilling the mitzvah of sukkah one merits sitting in the sukkah of Leviathan's skin.
records.originHebrew: וְהוּא בָּא אַחֲרֵי הַיְגִיעַ כַּפַּיִם בְּמַעֲשֶׂה, אַחַר כָּךְ מְהַנִּים אוֹתוֹ מִלְּמַעְלָה מֵעֵין עוֹלָם הַבָּא, וְאָז זוֹכֶה לְ"טוֹב לָךְ" גַּם בָּעוֹלָם הַבָּא:   (אות קמו) (מכתב יד קדשו).

records.themeTitle: The garment’s appearance and the soul’s root
records.themeSummary: A pleasing outward form and an inward spiritual quality are distinct matters.
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim develops the same verse about servants on horses and princes walking on the ground. Its contrast concerns the relation between outward garment and root: an attractive appearance can conceal a deficiency, while a coarse appearance can conceal a root without that deficiency. This explains the siman's distinction without making bodily appearance alone a reliable measure of a person's inward quality.
records.targetEnglish: Ashur and Egypt are alluded to in ‘I have seen servants on horses, and princes walking like servants on the earth’ (Ecclesiastes 10:7). My holy father explained: servants on horses indicate very beautiful and clean garments, while there is a deficiency at the root. As the Tikkunei Zohar says (Tikkun 60), evil within and a beautiful garment outside—of this it says, ‘I have seen servants on horses.’ Princes walking like servants on the earth indicate coarse and darkened garments, while at their root there is no deficiency.
records.originHebrew: דְּיֵשׁ נְפָשׁוֹת גְּדוֹלוֹת בְּגוּפִים מְכֹעָרִים, וְכֵן לְהֵיפֶךְ. וְהוּא סוֹד תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה וְשֶׁבִּכְתָב,

records.themeTitle: Purity within the same garment
records.themeSummary: The higher unity can reveal purity where the outward form had seemed to show its opposite.
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim explains the same question, ‘Who can bring pure from impure—is it not One?’ Its point is the disclosure of purity within the very garment that previously seemed impure, rather than merely replacing that garment. This develops why Rav Tzadok links the paradox to divine unity and why Bilaam's view of the outward act alone misses the source of its holiness.
records.targetEnglish: It is written (Job 14:4), ‘Who can bring pure from impure—is it not One?’ This means being able to see purity in the very form of the garment that previously appeared to show its opposite, without the garment itself changing. This is possible only when illumination shines from the highest place, called One, indicating One beyond reckoning: illumination from the higher will that is removed from all garments and free of all forms.

records.themeTitle: The given soul becomes one’s own world
records.themeSummary: The initial gift is attributed to the person through the work by which it is acquired.
records.explanation: Resisei Layla explains the transition from receiving a soul to calling its completed world one's own. The initial gift comes from Hashem; through Torah and mitzvot it becomes attributed to the person who has worked for it. This clarifies the siman's contrast between an insight that is only seen and a perfection that has become a settled acquisition.
records.targetEnglish: Just as Torah is initially ‘Hashem's Torah’ and afterward the person's Torah, so the soul begins with ‘He breathed into his nostrils,’ from Hashem, as we say, ‘The soul You gave me.’ At the end it is called the house of his own world, belonging to him: the soul is called by his name because through his effort he merited it. Thus the Sages said (Vayikra Rabbah 35), ‘As though you made yourselves,’ concerning ‘You shall perform them’ (Leviticus 26:3): through performing Torah and mitzvot one merits this.
records.originHebrew: וְצָרִיךְ הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת עַד שֶׁמַּגִּיעַ לִהְיוֹת כָּךְ בְּקִנְיָן וְנִבְלָע בַּלֵּב כָּל מַה שֶּׁמַּשִּׂיג, וְאָז נִקְרָא "קוֹנֶה עוֹלָמוֹ".
records.originEnglish: and one requires long exertion until he reaches the state where it becomes an internalized acquisition and all that he perceives is absorbed into his heart, and then he is termed "one who acquires his world."

records.targetRef: Sod Yesharim, The Seventh Day of Pesach 10:1
records.themeTitle: The prophet’s lament and the good still to be gathered
records.themeSummary: The fall of a counterpart can narrow a field of service while some good remains for later collection.
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim expressly explains the prophet's lament over another nation's fall: the corresponding field of human service becomes smaller when its opposing inclination disappears. Its Egypt example adds that some good remains to be gathered from a distance afterward. This develops the siman's reciprocal powers while preserving the reason for lament and the possibility of later collection.
records.targetEnglish: The matter is like what we find when a prophet foretold a nation's calamity: he lamented, as it says (Isaiah 15:5), ‘My heart cries out for Moav,’ and in chapter 16, ‘My innards sound like a harp for Moav, and my inward parts for Kir Cheres.’ He grieved over the nation's loss, because through this its inclination was annulled, and the power of service corresponding to that particular matter was thereby diminished. Yet in Egypt, although it says (Deuteronomy 17:16), ‘You shall not return by this way again’—even residence in Egypt was forbidden, alluding even to the inanimate—and the Sages said that it was made like a deep place without fish (Berakhot 9b), some points nevertheless remained there that would still enter holiness, to be gathered by Israel from a distance. Of them it says (Psalms 68:32), ‘Nobles will come from Egypt.’ As Pesachim 118b teaches: Egypt will bring a gift to Mashiach. He thinks he should not accept it, but the Holy One tells him to accept it, for they provided lodging for His children in Egypt. Immediately, ‘Nobles will come from Egypt.’
records.originHebrew: וּלְכָךְ יִרְמְיָה קוֹנֵן עַל אָבְדַן אֻמּוֹת עוֹבְדֵי כּוֹכָבִים, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "לִבִּי לְמוֹאָב יִזְעָק וְגוֹמֵר" (יְשַׁעְיָה טו, ה; יִרְמְיָה מח, לו), וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּבַמִּדְבָּר רַבָּה (רֵישׁ פָּרָשַׁת בָּלָק כ, א), וְהַיְינוּ שֶׁבְּאָבְדַן אוֹתָהּ אוּמָּה נִתְבַּטֵּל אוֹתוֹ כֹּחַ (כְּמוֹ שֶׁנִּתְבָּאֵר לְעֵיל אוֹת מ"ז, עַיֵּין שָׁם). וּבְכָל דָּבָר יֵשׁ גַּם כֵּן טוֹב כַּיָּדוּעַ, וְאָז נִתְרוֹמֵם אוֹתוֹ כֹּחַ הַטּוֹב.

records.targetRef: Likkutei Maamarim, On Book of Joshua 23
records.themeTitle: Accepted repentance and continuing recognition
records.themeSummary: Divine forgiveness and the person's renewed awareness of deficiency belong to different sides of repentance.
records.explanation: Likkutei Maamarim keeps together two statements that might appear to conflict: Hashem abundantly forgives, while the person continues to recognize his own failure. The distinction illuminates why a higher level can call forth renewed repentance without proving that the earlier repentance was rejected. The acknowledgment becomes more searching as the person's knowledge grows; the declaration that the past has been repaired remains a gift from Hashem rather than the person's self-exemption.
records.targetEnglish: This is why Hashem is called ‘the One who abundantly forgives’: forgiveness comes from His side, whereas from the human side there must be recognition of the sin and deficiency, as it says, ‘My sin is before me always’ (Psalms 51:5). Even though one confessed on this Yom Kippur, one confesses again on the next (Yoma 86b). For if a person decides for himself that there was no stumbling, but that everything was his own achievement, as do the nations around him, that itself is truly a stumbling. From the human side, one must recognize that a person has no independent power. The days when he walked in darkness, unaware that Hashem gives him the strength to act (Deuteronomy 8:18), were therefore sin and stumbling; then Hashem says that it was not a stumbling, as explained above.
records.originHebrew: סז] בְּכָל מַדְרֵגָה שֶׁהוּא עוֹלֶה, יֵשׁ לוֹ לַחֲזוֹר וְלָשׁוּב עַל חֲטָאָיו, וְזֶהוּ עִנְיַן "וְחַטָּאתִי נֶגְדִּי תָמִיד" (תְּהִלִּים נא, ה), אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהֶאֱמִין שֶׁכְּבָר נִתְקַבְּלָה תְּשׁוּבָתוֹ,

records.targetRef: Tiferet Yosef, Vayeilech and Shabbat Shuvah 3
records.themeTitle: What the commandments are counsels toward
records.themeSummary: The commandments train the embodied will to follow Hashem, beyond the presence of an isolated feeling.
records.explanation: Tiferet Yosef asks why all 613 commandments are called counsels: love and awe themselves are already included among the commandments, so neither alone explains what the complete set counsels a person toward. His answer is the alignment of the body and the will with Hashem's will. This deepens the siman's opening claim that bodily acts straighten the heart, and explains why the quiet inward attainment is the aim of their disciplined preparation.
records.targetEnglish: The 613 commandments are called in the holy Zohar (Yitro 82b) ‘613 counsels of the Torah.’ My holy father explained: toward what are they counsels? One cannot simply say that they are counsels toward love of Hashem, for love of Hashem is itself one of the 613 commandments. Fear of Hashem is likewise one of the 613 commandments. Rather, they are counsels by which a person's body is drawn after Hashem's will, so that there should be no inclination in his heart, Heaven forbid, contrary to Hashem's will.
records.originHebrew: סח] כָּל הָעֲבוֹדוֹת שֶׁבְּאֵבְרֵי הַגּוּף וְהַמִּצְווֹת שֶׁבָּהֶם הֵם רַק לְהַיְשִׁיר הַלֵּב, וְהָעִיקָּר הוּא הַלֵּב שֶׁשָּׁם מְעוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (שִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים רַבָּה ה, ב): הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לִבָּן שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "צוּר לְבָבִי וְגוֹמֵר". וּלְכָךְ לֹא יִהְיֶה זֶה הַמְּכֻוָּון מִן הָאָדָם, רַק כָּל אֵלֶּה דְּבָרִים הַמְּבִיאִים אֶל הַמְּכֻוָּון,
records.originEnglish: All forms of divine service performed through the bodily limbs and their commandments exist solely to rectify and align the heart; and the principal core is the heart, which is the dwelling place of the Blessed Name, as our Sages of blessed memory expounded (Shir HaShirim Rabbah 5:2): "The Holy One, blessed be He, is the heart of Israel, as it is stated: 'God is the rock of my heart, etc.'" (Psalms 73:26). Therefore the physical act itself should not be man's ultimate objective, but rather all these deeds are instruments leading to the ultimate goal,
records.targetHebrew: והתרי"ג מצות נקראים בזוה"ק (יתרו פ"ב:) תרי"ג עיטין דאורייתא. ואמר בזה כבוד אאמו"ר זללה"ה שלאיזה ענין הם עצות כי אין שייך לומר שהם עצות לאהבת ד' הלא אהבת ד' הוא ג"כ מצוה אחת מן התרי"ג מצות. וכן יראת ד' הוא ג"כ מצוה אחת מן התרי"ג מצות. ורק הם עצות לאדם להיות הגוף נמשך אחר רצון השי"ת, שלא יהיה לאדם שום נטיה בלב ח"ו להיפך מן רצונו של השי"ת.

records.themeTitle: Seeking the surviving point of good
records.themeSummary: The favorable judgment of the interpreters of the remnant develops a person's remaining good into a ground of advocacy.
records.explanation: Tiferet Yosef explains the very interpreters of the remnant invoked at the close of this siman. Their favorable reading is an active attempt to take hold of the surviving good and enlarge it, rather than a denial that a serious judgment was stated. This clarifies the order Rav Tzadok requires: the heart must first contain a real concern for the other's possible restoration before it can claim to speak only for justice.
records.targetEnglish: How far does the protection arising from the righteous person's service extend in this world? Even concerning those four individuals of whom the ruling states that they have no share in the world to come, the Gemara nevertheless teaches (Sanhedrin 104b) that the interpreters of the remnant said they do have a share. The interpreters of the remnant are the righteous who take hold of the point of Israel and extend it, advocating that none be utterly cast away. They are called interpreters of the remnant because they expound the remaining impression in the heart, until through their service they can protect even those four individuals and bring them to the life of the world to come. Thus the day of rain is greater, for it includes both righteous and wicked, whereas resurrection is for the righteous, since then evil is entirely annulled.
records.originHebrew: וְקוֹדֶם מִזְמוֹר זֶה נֶאֱמַר מִזְמוֹר שֶׁבּוֹ פָּסוּק "לִי גִלְעָד וְגוֹמֵר" (תְּהִלִּים קח, ט), שֶׁמִּמֶּנּוּ דָּרְשׁוּ דּוֹרְשֵׁי רְשׁוּמוֹת בְּפֶרֶק חֵלֶק (סַנְהֶדְרִין קד:) שֶׁכֻּלָּם יֵשׁ לָהֶם חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא, וְזֶהוּ כְּעֵין שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מְגִילָּה יג:) מִמִּדַּת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁמַּקְדִּים רְפוּאָה לַמַּכָּה. וְצָרִיךְ לְהַקְדִּים בְּלִבּוֹ הַטּוֹבַת עַיִן אֲפִילּוּ לָהֶם, וְאִם אַחַר כָּךְ מִכָּל מָקוֹם מְקַלְּלָם, אָז הוּא בְּמִשְׁפָּט:
records.originEnglish: And prior to this psalm comes the psalm containing the verse "Gilead is mine, etc." (Psalms 108:9), from which the masters of esoteric traces expounded in chapter Chelek (Sanhedrin 104b) that all those biblical sinners have a share in the World to Come, which mirrors what our Sages said (Megillah 13b) regarding the attribute of the Blessed Name, that He provides the cure before the blow. And one must first precede in his heart with a benevolent eye toward them, and if he nonetheless curses them afterward, it is then done with balanced justice.

records.themeTitle: A prophetic word can await its later hearers
records.themeSummary: Immediate resistance does not exhaust the effect of a prophetic teaching preserved for future generations.
records.explanation: Peri Tzadik explains why Jeremiah's resisted words can still be called words that are heard: their effect unfolds through later hearers. This strengthens the siman's distinction between an event's short duration and the continuing gateway it opens. It explains the premise about what is preserved for generations, while the siman itself goes on to distinguish the particular powers of Torah and prayer.
records.targetEnglish: Therefore the Gemara there cites the proof from the verse, “The end of the matter: everything is heard.” Even if it was not heard in its own time, in the end events will turn and unfold so that it is heard. As the Sages said (Megillah 14a), “A prophecy needed for generations was written,” and a time will come when it is heard.
records.originHebrew: וּכְבָר אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מְגִילָּה יד.): נְבוּאָה שֶׁהֻוצְרְכָה לְדוֹרוֹת נִכְתְּבָה, וְשֶׁלֹּא הֻוצְרְכָה לֹא נִכְתְּבָה; וְאִם כֵּן עַל כָּרְחֲךָ אוֹתָם סִפּוּרֵי הַמּוֹפְתִים הֵם צְרִיכִים לְדוֹרוֹת, וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהָיוּ רַק לְפִי שָׁעָה, הֵם פָּתְחוּ שְׁעָרִים בָּזֶה,
records.originEnglish: And our Sages already taught (Megillah 14a): A prophecy that was necessary for future generations was transcribed, while that which was not needed for posterity was not written down; and if so, perforce those accounts of their miracles are eternally needed for future generations, and even though they were temporary, they opened eternal spiritual gateways in this realm,

records.themeTitle: The visible birthright and its inward truth
records.themeSummary: Esav's outward precedence could be transferred because it did not express the inward root of the birthright.
records.explanation: Yisrael Kedoshim expands the compressed exception about selling Esav's birthright. It distinguishes priority in visible birth from the inward priority of formation, and describes Esav's connection to Avraham as dependent on an outward bodily garment. This makes precise why the siman can treat that sale as effective without making intrinsic holiness generally saleable.
records.targetEnglish: Yaakov was first in formation—that is, in the truth concealed in this world. But in the visible disclosure of this world, in birth, Esav appeared first, for the service is in deed and the power of action, and Esav is the root of the power of deeds. As long as Avraham our father himself was alive, clothed in a physical body in this world, there was also a physical garment of his level in Esav because of the mixture of good and evil in the bodily world. But at Avraham's passing, when his spiritual holiness remained without a physical garment in this world, Esav no longer had a connection with it, since all his power belongs to physical embodiment in this world. Through that embodiment he could extend his hooves and display himself as pure, for this world is a world of falsehood; this is not so from the standpoint of ‘truth to Yaakov’ (Micah 7:20). Yaakov therefore received the spiritual dimension alone, and then ‘Yaakov cooked a stew’ (Genesis 25:29).
records.originHebrew: וְעִנְיַן מְכִירַת הַבְּכוֹרָה דְּעֵשָׂו לְהַקְרִיב קָרְבָּנוֹת, שֶׁנִּרְאֶה כִּמְכִירַת דָּבָר קְדוּשָׁה, שָׁמַעְתִּי לְפִי שֶׁהוּא הָיָה בְּכוֹר בְּדִמְיוֹן וְלֹא בֶּאֱמֶת, לְפִיכָךְ הוֹעִילָה מְכִירָה בְּדִמְיוֹן.
records.originEnglish: And regarding the sale of the birthright by Esau to offer sacrifices, which appears like the sale of a sacred matter, I heard: because he was a firstborn only in illusion and not in truth, therefore a sale within the realm of illusion was effective.

records.themeTitle: The enduring root of the bond
records.themeSummary: The holiness described as intrinsic rests on a bond that changing outward actions cannot simply exchange.
records.explanation: Beit Yaakov develops the same verse about love that many waters cannot extinguish, locating the bond with Avraham in divine choice at a level beyond the reach of changing actions. This clarifies the root of the siman's analogy to intrinsic sanctity. The parallel explains the endurance of the bond; it does not cancel the siman's distinction between the person's true possession and the sins from which he still requires redemption.
records.targetEnglish: The matter is that Hashem bound His love to Avraham our father in a place beyond the reach of human actions. As the holy Zohar teaches (Bereshit 22b), ‘He is One, without reckoning and without partnership’; this love endures forever. Of this love it is said, ‘Many waters cannot extinguish love’ (Song of Songs 8:7), for no action reaches that place so as to extinguish it. As the Midrash Tanchuma says (Tzav 8), ‘He chose Avraham’: after the Akeidah, the love and bond Hashem has with Avraham our father were revealed even apart from his good deeds, through the choice by which He chose him from birth, as it says, ‘Who chose Avram’ (Nehemiah 9:7).
records.originHebrew: אֲבָל הַמִּצְווֹת הֵם קְדוּשַׁת הַגּוּף וְאֵין לָהֶם פִּדְיוֹן. וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "אִם יִתֵּן אִישׁ אֶת כָּל הוֹן בֵּיתוֹ בָּאַהֲבָה בּוֹז יָבוּזוּ לוֹ]". וְעַיֵּין בִּתְשׁוּבוֹת רַב הַאי גָּאוֹן שֶׁהֵבִיא מַהֲרַ״ם אַלְשַׁקַּר בְּעִנְיַן אֶחָד שֶׁמָּכַר מִצְווֹתָיו דְּאֵין מוֹעִיל, עַיֵּין שָׁם.
records.originEnglish: However, the mitzvot possess bodily sanctity (kedushat haguf), and they are not subject to redemption. And as it is written: 'If a man would give all the wealth of his house for love, it would be utterly scorned' (Song of Songs 8:7). And see the Responsa of Rav Hai Gaon cited by Maharam Alashkar regarding one who sold his mitzvot, that it is completely ineffective, see there.
records.targetHebrew: וְהָעִנְיָן הוּא, שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ קָשַׁר אַהֲבָתוֹ לְאַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ בְּמָקוֹם שֶׁאֵין מַגִּיעִים שָׁם מַעֲשֵׂי בְּנֵי אָדָם, וְכִדְאִיתָא בַּזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ בְּרֵאשִׁית (דַּף כב:): אֲבָל אִיהוּ חַד בְּלָא חוּשְׁבָּן וּבְלָא שִׁתּוּף (וְעַיֵּין שָׁם כָּל הָעִנְיָן), וְהִיא הַמִּתְקַיֶּמֶת לָעַד. וְעַל זוֹ הָאַהֲבָה נֶאֱמַר (שִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים ח׳:ז׳): מַיִם רַבִּים לֹא יוּכְלוּ לְכַבּוֹת אֶת הָאַהֲבָה, כִּי לְשָׁם אֵין מַגִּיעַ שׁוּם מַעֲשֶׂה שֶׁתּוּכַל לְכַבּוֹתָהּ, וְכִדְאִיתָא בְּמִדְרַשׁ תַּנְחוּמָא (פָּרָשַׁת צַו ח): אַבְרָהָם בְּחָרוֹ, וְהַיְינוּ שֶׁאַחַר הָעֲקֵידָה נִתְגַּלָּה הָאַהֲבָה וְהַהִתְקַשְּׁרוּת שֶׁיֵּשׁ לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ עִם אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם אַף בְּלֹא פְּעוּלוֹתָיו הַטּוֹבִים, רַק מִטַּעַם בְּחִירָה שֶׁבָּחַר בּוֹ מִיּוֹם הִוָּלְדוֹ, כִּדְכְתִיב (נְחֶמְיָה ט׳:ז׳): אֲשֶׁר בָּחַרְתָּ בְּאַבְרָם.

records.targetRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Lech Lecha 6
records.themeTitle: A future good concealed within an unexpected rescue
records.themeSummary: The later Davidic line can make an initially puzzling preservation intelligible.
records.explanation: Mei HaShiloach describes Shem's difficulty with Avraham's rescue of Lot: Ammon and Moab seemed to make the rescue an obstacle to Jerusalem's future. The answer appears through the permitted female lines from which David and Shlomo emerge. This is a close structural parallel to the siman's Menashe example: a visible failure in one generation does not disclose the whole future of the line. The qualification concerning male and female descendants is retained in the quotation.
records.targetEnglish: When Shem saw his disciple Avraham go to rescue Lot, he could not understand the act according to his own judgment. Seemingly he should not have helped him, since Ammon and Moab would emerge from him, troublesome neighbors of Jerusalem (Sanhedrin 96b), and Hashem had warned that they should not enter the congregation. Why, then, did Avraham risk his life to rescue him? But Shem knew Avraham as his disciple and recognized him as thoroughly righteous, so that surely no stumbling would come through him. He prayed to Hashem to illuminate his eyes and disclose the reason for Avraham's act. Thus it says, ‘He was a priest to God Most High’: when he brought out the bread and wine he was serving Hashem and praying that He illuminate his eyes to understand what lay beyond his own intellect and comprehension. Hashem then illuminated his eyes to show that nothing had been done through Avraham in vain. Although Ammon and Moab would emerge from Lot and were told not to enter (Lamentations 1:10), this restriction concerned the males; the females were permitted immediately. From them would emerge the kingship of David and Shlomo, the principal support of the kingship of the land of Israel and Jerusalem. Therefore he said, ‘Blessed is Avram to God Most High.’
records.originHebrew: וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ לְחִזְקִיָּהוּ פֶּרֶק קַמָּא דִּבְרָכוֹת (י.): בַּהֲדֵי כַּבְשֵׁי דְּרַחֲמָנָא לְמָא לָךְ? וַהֲרֵי מְנַשֶּׁה מֵאוֹתָן שֶׁאֵין לָהֶם חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא, וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם הָיָה נֶאֱבַד חַס וְשָׁלוֹם מָשִׁיחַ בֶּן דָּוִד וְכָל הַשַּׁלְשֶׁלֶת הַקְּדוֹשָׁה מִן הָעוֹלָם אִלּוּ לֹא נוֹלַד. וּמָצִינוּ "וַיִּקֹּד הָעָם וַיִּשְׁתַּחֲווּ" בְּפָרָשַׁת בֹּא, וּפֵירֵשׁ רַשִּׁ"י: שָׂמְחוּ עַל בְּשׂוֹרַת הַבָּנִים; וַהֲרֵי שָׁם הוּא בִּשְׁאֵלַת "מָה הָעֲבֹדָה הַזֹּאת לָכֶם", שֶׁהוּא שְׁאֵלַת בֵּן רָשָׁע כִּדְאִיתָא בַּהַגָּדָה: "וְאַף אַתָּה הַקְהֵה וְכוּלֵי", וַאֲפִילּוּ הָכִי שָׂמְחוּ עַל בְּשׂוֹרַת לֵידָתוֹ. וּמִיהוּ בַּמִּדְרָשׁ (תַּנְחוּמָא תְּרוּמָה ט) מְפוֹרָשׁ לְהֵיפֶךְ עַיֵּין שָׁם, דִּתְפִלַּת שְׁלֹמֹה הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם שֶׁאִם יְבַקֵּשׁ בֵּן וְהוּא יִהְיֶה רָשָׁע – לֹא יִתֵּן לוֹ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ:
records.originEnglish: And concerning this they said to Hezekiah in the first chapter of Berakhot (10a): "Why do you meddle in the secrets of the Merciful One?"; for behold, Manasseh was counted among those who have no share in the World to Come, yet nonetheless the Messiah son of David and the entire holy lineage would have been lost from the world, Heaven forbid, had he not been born. And we find "and the people bowed their heads and worshipped" in Parashat Bo (Exodus 12:27), where Rashi explains: they rejoiced over the tidings of future children; yet there it is framed in the question "What is this service to you?", which is the question of the wicked son as brought in the Haggadah: "you too blunt his teeth, etc.", and even so, they rejoiced over the tidings of his birth. However, in the Midrash (Tanchuma, Terumah 9) it is explicitly stated to the contrary, see there: that King Solomon, peace be upon him, prayed that if he should request a son who would turn out wicked, the Blessed Name should not grant him one.
records.targetHebrew: ולכן כאשר ראה שאברהם תלמידו הלך להציל את לוט, אשר כפי משפט דעתו והבנתו לא נודע לו מה זאת, הלא אדרבה, מהראוי היה שלא לעזרו, כי יצמח מאתו עמון ומואב אשר המה שיבבי בישא דירושלים (סנהדרין צו עמוד ב), וגם ה' שונא אותם כי הזהיר עליהם שלא יבאו בקהל, ואיך מסר אברהם אבינו עליו השלום את נפשו עליו להצילו?! אך לפי שידע את אברהם תלמידו והכיר אותו לצדיק גמור, ומסתמא לא יאנה לו שום מכשול, התפלל להשם יתברך שיאור עיניו בזה להודיע לו סבת מעשה אברהם אבינו עליו השלום; ולזאת נאמר: "והוא כהן לאל עליון", היינו בשעת הוצאת הלחם והיין אז היה כהן עובד להשם יתברך ומתפלל אליו, שיאיר עיניו למען ידע הדברים על מכונם אשר המה למעלה משכלו והשגתו. ואחר זה האיר השם יתברך את עיניו להראות לו כי חס ושלום לא נעשה על ידי אברהם אבינו עליו השלום שום דבר לבטלה, כי אף אמנם שמלוט יצאו עמון ומואב שנאמר עליהם (איכה א, י): "לא יבאו וכולי", רק זאת הוא הזכרים, אבל נקבותיהם מותרות מיד, ואדרבה, מזה נצמח מלכות בית דוד ושלמה אשר הם עיקר קיום מלוכת ארץ ישראל וירושלים; ולזאת אמר: "ברוך אברם לאל עליון".

records.themeTitle: Diminished reception does not diminish the source
records.themeSummary: The eclipse analogy distinguishes the light itself from its disclosure to those below.
records.explanation: Kometz HaMinchah explicitly develops the same source-and-recipient distinction. Its alternative explanation treats the sun's eclipse as an absence of light for observers while the light remains complete at its source. This helps specify what the siman means by a blemish above: the intended disclosure and reception are impaired, and that impairment is described in relation to the source's purpose of giving light.
records.targetEnglish: Alternatively: when the moon is eclipsed, the light is absent in the moon itself. This is an unfavorable sign for Israel, as it says, ‘I am with him in distress’ (Psalms 91:15), and when the Temple was destroyed the heavenly retinue was diminished. But an eclipse of the sun is an absence of light for those who see it, rather than in the sun. This is an unfavorable sign for the nations: the flow remains complete in its own place, but is lacking for them.
records.originHebrew: עט] עִנְיַן הַפְּגָם לְמַעְלָה עַל יְדֵי עֲווֹנוֹת הוּא עַל דֶּרֶךְ מַה שֶּׁאָנוּ אוֹמְרִים שֶׁהַחַמָּה לוֹקָה; וּבֶאֱמֶת הַחַמָּה בְּעַצְמוּתָהּ וּמִצִּידָּהּ אֵינָהּ לוֹקָה כְּלָל, רַק הֶעְדֵּר אוֹרָהּ לָאָרֶץ – זֶה מִקְרֵי לַקּוּת לַחַמָּה, שֶׁהֲרֵי עִנְיַן תַּכְלִיתָהּ שֶׁל חַמָּה לְהָאִיר לָאָרֶץ, וְזֶה לַקּוּת מִצִּידָּהּ.
records.originEnglish: The concept of a spiritual blemish Above caused by sins operates along the lines of what we say when the sun suffers an eclipse; for in truth, the sun in its own essence and from its own perspective suffers no eclipse whatsoever, only that the withholding of its light from reaching the earth is termed an eclipse of the sun, seeing that the ultimate purpose of the sun is to illuminate the earth, and this constitutes a failure from its functional side.

records.themeTitle: Gilead and the distinct uses of severity
records.themeSummary: The existence of a holy counterpart does not make every expression of anger holy.
records.explanation: Peri Tzadik develops the same connection between Gilead, refuge cities, and anger through Moshe's burial there. It also distinguishes the specific task of Pinchas from Moshe's own exceptional purity, including the consequence of even a slight appearance of anger. That distinction helps explain why the siman's account of a holy root of severity cannot be used to justify Ahab's claim that his killing was therefore holy.
records.targetEnglish: Moshe our teacher was also entirely clear of anger, without the slightest trace of it. Therefore, in this portion, when a slight appearance of displeasure was seen in him and he departed from his measure by a small amount, as it says, ‘Moshe became angry,’ the law of purifying Midian's vessels was concealed from him. He was thereby shown the need for care even in a very subtle matter, just as a vessel requires purification and immersion even after only a short time in gentile possession. In the incident of Zimri he was shown that a particular need can sometimes require precisely the use of anger and zeal. The law concerning the zealots was therefore concealed from him, since this act of zeal did not belong to his own task; Pinchas came and took what was fitting for him. For this reason, too, Moshe's burial was east of the Jordan in Gad's portion: ‘there the lawgiver's portion is concealed.’ The Sages teach (Makkot 9b) that three refuge cities were needed there because murderers were numerous in Gilead, the opposing husk of anger and zeal. Moshe, who was wholly pure in this respect, was buried there to subdue that opposing counterpart, as explained concerning his burial opposite Beit Peor.
records.originHebrew: פ] תִּיקּוּן לְכַעַס – שִׁינּוּי מָקוֹם, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרָה תּוֹרָה גָּלוּת לְרוֹצֵחַ וְהָיָה עִיר מִקְלָט וְלֹא נָע וָנָד לְעוֹלָם, כִּי בֶּאֱמֶת יֵשׁ פַּחַד יִצְחָק וּגְבוּרוֹת קְדוֹשׁוֹת שֶׁטּוֹב, כְּעִנְיַן הַאי צוּרְבָּא מֵרַבָּנָן דְּרָתַח (תַּעֲנִית ד.), וְזֶהוּ הָעִיר מִקְלָט. וּבְגִלְעָד וּשְׁכֶם דִּשְׁכִיחֵי רוֹצְחִים הִרְבּוּ עָרֵי מִקְלָט כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּמַכּוֹת (ט סוֹף עַמּוּד ב), כִּי אֵין הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בָּא בִּטְרוּנְיָא;
records.originEnglish: The spiritual rectification for anger is change of place, just as the Torah prescribed exile for an unintentional murderer and he was granted a City of Refuge rather than wandering aimlessly forever, for in truth there is the holy 'Fear of Isaac' and sacred Gevurot which are good, in the manner of a young Torah scholar who flares up in holy wrath (Ta'anit 4a), and this is the City of Refuge. records.themeTitle: Another person's task can complete the same service
records.themeSummary: Making room for another's visible contribution can express a deeper recognition of the whole.
records.explanation: Tiferet Yosef supplies an account of the inward recognition that opposes envy: those making the ark and those making the curtains discover the honor of Heaven in one another's different tasks. This illuminates the disposition sought in the siman's succession argument. A person's own visible prominence can recede while the shared service continues through another; the source develops that relation through concrete complementary roles rather than merely advising a general feeling of goodwill.
records.targetEnglish: The counsel for this is the commandment of Hakhel. Men, women, and children were present, as the Gemara teaches (Chagigah 3a): the men come to learn, the women to hear; why do the children come? To give reward to those who bring them. Through Hakhel a person recognizes that even Israel's little children, who do not yet learn or hear, nevertheless have the power to give reward to those who bring them. No member of Israel can simply be treated as deficient. Thus ‘Moshe assembled’ is also written before the completion of the Mishkan, for there this recognition was explicit. As my holy grandfather explained in Mei HaShiloach (Volume I, Vayakhel, under ‘Vayakhel’), although one made the ark, another the curtain, and others the boards and hangings, afterward all recognized that the honor of Heaven coming through the maker of the ark also comes through the maker of the hangings. They recognized how each clarified the other. Once they recognized this, they became the vessel in which Hashem would rest His presence.
records.originHebrew: [פא] פְּעָמִים נִגְזַר עַל אָדָם לָמוּת חַס וְשָׁלוֹם מִשּׁוּם "אֵין מַלְכוּת וְכוּלֵי", כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם וּמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם; וְהָעֵצָה לָזֶה – הֶעְדֵּר הַקִּנְאָה, וְשֶׁיַּסְכִּים שֶׁיַּאֲפִיל הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ אוֹרוֹ בְּחַיָּיו וְיִזְרַח אוֹר אַחֵר,
records.originEnglish: Sometimes it is decreed upon a person to die, Heaven forbid, because "one kingdom does not overlap another," as found with King David and Moses our teacher; and the spiritual counsel for this is the eradication of envy, willingly consenting that the Blessed Name dim his light during his lifetime while another light shines forth,

records.themeTitle: The find exceeds what effort could specify
records.themeSummary: Preparation does not give a person control over the particular insight that is afterward received.
records.explanation: Peri Tzadik explains why attainment after labor is still called a find: before attaining the insight, a person could not have aimed his effort at that unknown insight itself. This clarifies the siman's distinction between working and sitting in expectation of a windfall. The effort prepares a recipient; the particular disclosure remains a gift beyond what the recipient could previously describe or demand.
records.targetEnglish: The meaning of the expression ‘you found’ is well known: a find comes unexpectedly (Sanhedrin 97a). The attainment afterward comes as a find, for a person attains something toward which he had not directed his labor at all. Before the attainment, he could not have labored toward an attainment of that kind. Rather, when someone labors in words of Torah, Hashem bestows and gives him wisdom to attain even what is above his own wisdom and comprehension. As the Gemara teaches (Bava Batra 12a): know that this is so, for a great scholar states a teaching, and it is found that a tradition given to Moshe at Sinai accords with him.
records.originHebrew: וּכְעִנְיַן "וְנֹחַ מָצָא חֵן בְּעֵינֵי ה'", וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה כט): הוּא מָצָא, אֲבָל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לֹא מָצָא; הַיְינוּ כִּי פְּעָמִים אָדָם זוֹכֶה בְּלֹא שׁוּם יְגִיעָה שֶׁהוּא שָׁמוּר מִן הָעֲבֵירָה וְנִקְרָא צַדִּיק, וְזֶהוּ מַדְרֵגַת נֹחַ שֶׁמִּדָּה כְּנֶגֶד מִדָּה הָיָה שָׁמוּר מִן הַפּוּרְעָנִיּוֹת]. וּפְעָמִים אָדָם זוֹכֶה לְהַשִּׂיג הַשָּׂגוֹת מִידִיעַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ וְאוֹרוֹ, וְזֶהוּ מְצִיאַת יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מָצָא, שֶׁבָּזֶה מְיוּחָס גַּם כֵּן הַמְּצִיאָה לְמַעְלָה, כִּי יוֹתֵר מִמַּה שֶּׁעֵגֶל וְכוּלֵי כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי לְעֵיל אוֹת ע"ט.
records.originEnglish: and along the lines of "And Noah found grace in the eyes of Hashem" (Genesis 6:8), concerning which our Sages expounded (Bereishit Rabbah 29:1): he found grace, but the Holy One, blessed be He, did not find grace in him; that is, because sometimes a person merits without any strenuous effort to be preserved from sin and is titled a righteous man, which was the level of Noah who, measure for measure, was preserved from the cataclysmic punishment. And at other times a person merits to attain profound perceptions of the knowledge of the Blessed Name and His light, and this is the "finding" of Israel which the Holy One, blessed be He, found, in which this discovery is likewise attributed to Above, for "more than the calf desires to suckle, the cow desires to nurse," as I wrote above in Section 79.

records.themeTitle: A personal repair and its comparative effect
records.themeSummary: The same righteous act can repair its doer while exposing an unresolved contrast with others.
records.explanation: Yisrael Kedoshim develops the difficult distinction through Mordechai: an encounter could provide the occasion of his own repentance while also occasioning prosecution against others. This gives a concrete explanation of why the siman can describe a consequence as apparently unjust without denying hidden judgment. The originating siman's conclusion remains essential: motives can be hidden even from their owner, and its stated response is prayer for mercy.
records.targetEnglish: For Mordechai himself, this was a repair for his participation in the feast. Presumably he had also been among those who bowed to the image, for he had already been exiled with Yechonyah (Esther 2:6) and was one of the Men of the Great Assembly; the Rambam writes that they were all included apart from Chananyah, Mishael, and Azaryah. When a Torah scholar has sinned, do not suspect him afterward, for he has certainly repented (Berakhot 19a). Yet repentance requires that the matter be occasioned for him and that he emerge from it without failure (Yoma 86b). Mordechai was presented with the matter of Haman and recognized that Hashem had placed it before him to repair the sin of the feast. He therefore devoted himself to it and repaired himself, becoming the one prepared for this redemption. Nevertheless, he brought some difficulty upon others: that act occasioned the decree, because it aroused prosecution against Israel. This resembles the widow's words to Eliyahu, ‘Have you come to remind me of my sin and cause my son's death?’ (I Kings 17:18) When one person is exceptionally righteous, the contrast can arouse prosecution against those with him who are not at that level.
records.originHebrew: [פד] פְּעָמִים יֵשׁ "נִסְפֶּה בְּלֹא מִשְׁפָּט" (מִשְׁלֵי יג, כג), הַיְינוּ עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ: "יֵשׁ צַדִּיק אֹבֵד בְּצִדְקוֹ" (קֹהֶלֶת ז, טו) – עַל יְדֵי צִדְקוּתוֹ, כְּמוֹ הֶבֶל שֶׁהֲרָגוֹ קַיִן בִּשְׁבִיל שֶׁקִּבֵּל ה' מִנְחָתוֹ; וּבְוַדַּאי הָיָה הֲרִיגָה זוֹ מִמִּשְׁפַּט הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.
records.originEnglish: Sometimes there is one who is "swept away without justice" (Proverbs 13:23), which operates along the lines of "there is a righteous man who perishes in his righteousness" (Ecclesiastes 7:15)—specifically on account of his righteousness, like Abel whom Cain murdered because Hashem accepted his offering; and certainly this slaying was part of the ultimate judgment of the Blessed Name.

records.targetRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Bereshit 3
records.themeTitle: A share in the creatures and their return to the source
records.themeSummary: Human service can elevate the powers received from the rest of creation.
records.explanation: Mei HaShiloach gives the mechanism behind the shared life described here: the human being receives powers from the inanimate, growing, and animal worlds, and through service returns them to Hashem. Its conclusion that the creatures share in the human being's good and harm makes the relation reciprocal. This helps explain why the siman treats one's associated creatures as an occasion for examining one's own service rather than as spiritually detached possessions.
records.targetEnglish: ‘God said, Let us make man.’ At first Hashem created all the creatures. Then the creatures understood and recognized their lack: they had no one to connect their life to Hashem. Through the human being all the things of this world are connected to Hashem, for he elevates everything. The inanimate gives its power to the growing, the growing to the living, and the living to the speaking human. When the human being serves Hashem with that strength, he elevates all the powers he received from this world, even the power of the inanimate. When the creatures perceived their lack, their collective power aroused the awakening above for the creation of humanity. ‘God said, Let us make man’ means that Hashem told all the creatures to contribute their powers and join in humanity's creation, so that the human being would have a share in all of them. When he needs something they can all assist him, since his harm also harms them, as in the generation of the Flood, and his good also benefits them.
records.originHebrew: [פו] כָּל מַה שֶּׁהוּא מִקִּנְיַן הָאָדָם: אִשְׁתּוֹ וּבָנָיו, עַבְדּוֹ וַאֲמָתוֹ, שׁוֹרוֹ וַחֲמוֹרוֹ, אָהֳלוֹ וְכַסְפּוֹ וּזְהָבוֹ וְכָל אֲשֶׁר לוֹ – הַכֹּל הוּא מִשּׁוֹרֶשׁ נַפְשׁוֹ, כִּי גַּם כָּל הַדּוֹמֵם, צוֹמֵחַ, חַי מְשׁוֹרָשִׁים בְּנֶפֶשׁ הָאָדָם וְשׁוֹרֶשׁ חַיּוּתָם מִמֶּנּוּ כַּנּוֹדָע. וּמַה שֶּׁקָּנוּי לוֹ הוּא שֶׁשּׁוֹרֶשׁ חַיּוּתָם מִמֶּנּוּ,
records.originEnglish: Everything that belongs to a person's possessions—his wife and children, his manservant and maidservant, his ox and donkey, his tent, his silver and gold, and all that he owns—all derives from the root of his soul; for all inanimate matter, vegetation, and animal life are rooted in the human soul, and the source of their vitality stems from him, as is known. And that which is acquired by him is because the root of their vitality flows directly from his soul;

"וַיֹּאמֶר אֱלֹקִים נַעֲשֶׂה אָדָם", הַיְינוּ שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ אָמַר לְכָל הַבְּרִיּוֹת שֶׁכֻּלָּם יִתְּנוּ מִכֹּחָם וְיִצְטָרְפוּ לִבְרִיאַת הָאָדָם לְמַעַן יִהְיֶה לָאָדָם חֵלֶק בְּכֻלָּם, בִּכְדֵי שֶׁאִם יִצְטָרֵךְ הָאָדָם לִדְבַר מָה יַעַמְדוּ כֻּלָּם לַעֲזֹר לוֹ כִּי בְּרָעָתוֹ יֵרַע לָהֶם גַּם כֵּן כְּמוֹ בְּדוֹר הַמַּבּוּל, וּבְטוֹבָתוֹ יוּטַב גַּם לָהֶם.

records.targetRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Exodus, Bo 4
records.themeTitle: What fills the heart after a desire is removed
records.themeSummary: A straight path requires an inward direction that can replace the rejected desire.
records.explanation: Mei HaShiloach explains why merely finding one’s conduct unobstructed is insufficient. Avoiding a bad desire for convenience can leave the heart available to another bad desire; love of Hashem changes what fills the space. This develops Rav Tzadok’s counsel to examine the heart when a path seems straight: the inward motive, rather than the feeling of ease, determines the character of the path.
records.targetEnglish: It is written (Proverbs 15:19), ‘The way of the lazy is like a hedge of thorns, but the path of the upright is paved.’ The way of the lazy means this: even if a person restrains himself from bad actions, bad thoughts, and bad desires, if he does so without love of Hashem but rather as a lazy person—for example, understanding that such things will not succeed for him in this world, or for another reason that is not love of Hashem—his way is like a hedge of thorns. The heart cannot be empty of thoughts and desires even for a moment. When thoughts of craving leave his heart, a thought of anger or the like enters it. All his ways are like a hedge of thorns: he will always need self-restraint and effort; before one thing leaves his heart, another improper thing enters. But ‘the path of the upright’ means turning away from everything because of love of Hashem. His path is paved toward the good, because when a bad thing leaves his heart, love of Hashem remains there, and consequently nothing else improper will enter his heart.
records.originHebrew: וּמִי שֶׁבְּעֵינָיו הוּא יָשָׁר, מַה יַּעֲשֶׂה? וַהֲלֹא לְפִי דַעְתּוֹ הוֹלֵךְ בְּיֹשֶׁר! עַל זֶה אָמַר: "וְתֹכֵן לִבּוֹת ה'", מִי שֶׁלִּבּוֹ שָׁלֵם אֵין הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מַשְׁגֵּהוּ לְהַטְעוֹתוֹ, וְאֵינוֹ בָּא בִּטְרוּנְיָא, רַק עַקְמוּמִית שֶׁבַּלֵּב הוּא הַגּוֹרֵם הַטָּעוּת:
records.originEnglish: And if in a man's own eyes his way appears straight, what can he do, since according to his own judgment he is walking uprightly? Concerning this Scripture concludes: "but Hashem weighs the hearts" (Proverbs 21:2): one whose heart is wholly sincere, the Blessed Name will not mislead into error, nor does He act tyrannically; rather, an unrectified crookedness within the heart is what triggers the intellectual mistake.
records.targetHebrew: כתיב (משלי טית ואו, יוד טית) "דרך עצל כמשכת חדק וארח ישרים סלולה". דרך עצל הינו אף שאדם מונע את עצמו ממעשים רעים וממחשבות רעות ורצונות רעות, אף שאינו עושה זאת מחמת אהבת השם יתברך רק עושה כעצל, כגון שמבין שבעולם הזה לא יצלחו לו דברים כאלה, או באפן אחר שאינו מאהבת השם יתברך, אז דרכו הוא כמשכת חדק, כי הלב לא יוכל להיות פנוי ממחשבות ורצונות אף רגע אחת, וכאשר יסור מחשבות תאוה מלבו יבא ללבו מחשבת כעס וכדומה, וכל דרכיה המה כמשכת חדק, כי לעולם יצטרך לסגוף ועבודה קדם שיסור דבר אחד מלבו יבא ללבו דבר אחר שאינו הגון. אבל "ארח ישרים" הינו שפונה מכל דבר מחמת אהבת השם יתברך, זה הוא דרכו סלול לטוב, כי כאשר יסור מלבו איזה דבר רע ישאר בלבו אהבת השם יתברך, וממילא לא יבא ללבו שום דבר אחר שלא כהוגן.

records.themeTitle: When ordinary conversation is shaped by Torah
records.themeSummary: Speech becomes consistently directed toward Torah through chosen dedication, rather than an automatic status.
records.explanation: Sichat Malakhei HaSharet explains the same teaching about a scholar's ordinary conversation as Torah. It describes a mouth so devoted to Torah that even unplanned speech carries that direction, while expressly preserving the speaker's choice and the possibility of failing to live that role. This supplies the mechanism for the siman's second explanation: Torah heals and opens the tongue by changing the source from which its speech emerges.
records.targetEnglish: The meaning is: do not think that the separation of the tribe of Levi is an inborn statute, as though they were created like angels with no possibility of being otherwise. That would remove their choice. Rather, the description applies when Torah comes forth from a person's mouth. ‘Comes forth’ means almost of itself: his mouth has become so fully a sheath for words of Torah that Torah comes forth from it of itself, for his lips speak only Torah, even without a particular prior intention. This is like the teaching (Sukkah 21b), ‘Its leaf shall not wither’—even the ordinary conversation of Torah scholars. When his lips utter nothing detached from Torah, he is like the ministering angels, dedicated to Hashem's mission, all the thoughts of his heart in this world directed to that task. Otherwise, the opposite description applies.
records.originHebrew: מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן שֶׁלֹּא לְדַבֵּר כְּלָל. אִי נַמֵּי: עֵצָה הוּא אֵיךְ יוּכַל לְאֻמָּנוּת זוֹ כְּשֶׁ"צֶדֶק תְּדַבֵּרוּן", כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּעֵרָכִין (טו:) וּבִדְבָרִים רַבָּה (רֵישׁ פָּרָשָׁה א) שֶׁדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה מַרְפֵּא הַלָּשׁוֹן;
records.originEnglish: unlike staying completely silent, which is simple. Alternatively, it provides counsel on how to acquire this craft of speaking righteousness, as written in Arachin 15b and Devarim Rabbah 1:1, that words of Torah heal the tongue;
records.targetHebrew: יאמר זה, שאל תחשב שהבדלת שבט הלוי הוא חקה שהם נבראו כך כמלאכים שאין בידם שלא להיות מלאכים, שאם כן תסלק הבחירה מהם, רק כאשר התורה יוצאה מפיו; ואמר "יוצאה", כאלו יוצאה מעצמה, שכל כך נעשה פיו נרתק לדברי תורה עד שדברי תורה יוצאה מעצמה מפיו, כי אין שפתותיו דובבות אלא דברי תורה, וגם שלא במתכון; ועל דרך שאיתא (סכה כ״א עמוד ב׳): "'ועלהו לא יבול' — אפילו שיחת חלין וכולי", כי אין שפתותיהם רוחשות כלל דברים שאינם דברי תורה, אז הוא כמלאכי השרת, שמתיחד בשליחות השם יתברך, שכל מחשבות לבבו בעולם הזה רק לזה, ואם לאו וכולי.

records.targetRef: Sod Yesharim, The Seventh Night of Pesach 11:1
records.themeTitle: The inward form of a generation and its outward counterpart
records.themeSummary: Changes in the generation's spiritual form are reflected in the form of its opposition.
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim develops the same concluding rabbinic proverb through Eliyahu and Ahab. A storm-like divine garment is expressed in the righteous figure and met by a corresponding storm of opposition; when the form of governance changes, neither response simply continues unchanged. This gives a concrete model of the siman's claim that the changing Torah and souls of a generation are reflected in the changing world around them.
records.targetEnglish: ‘When Pharaoh sent out the people, God did not lead them by the way of the land of the Philistines, although it was near.’ It is written (Proverbs 10), ‘When the storm passes, the wicked is no more, but the righteous is an everlasting foundation.’ My holy grandfather explained that Hashem has a garment called storm, as it says, ‘Hashem's way is in storm and tempest.’ When Hashem governs the upper worlds through that garment, the righteous foundation of the world is likewise clothed in it here. Thus Eliyahu said in his generation, ‘I have been exceedingly zealous for Hashem, God of hosts, for Israel has forsaken Your covenant.’ Opposite the righteous person clothed in storm and tempest stands the contrary force with its storm of expansive assertion, as Ahab stood opposite Eliyahu. Afterward, when Hashem removes that garment from the order of His governance and begins to govern gently, Eliyahu is told (Zohar, Vayigash 209b) that the world cannot endure his manner among people. The storm and noise of the opposing force likewise quiet down, as the Sages said (Chagigah 5b), ‘When counsel is lost from the children, their wisdom decays.’ Whoever remains opposed to that new governance loses his standing entirely.
records.originHebrew: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁהַנְּפָשׁוֹת מִשְׁתַּנּוֹת מִדּוֹר לְדוֹר, כֵּן הַתּוֹרָה, וְהַיְינוּ הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה שֶׁמִּתְחַדֵּשׁ בְּכָל דּוֹר חֲדָשׁוֹת עַל יְדֵי חַכְמֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל; וְעַל יְדֵי כָּל חֲדָשׁוֹת הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה יוֹצֵא לָאוֹר נְפָשׁוֹת חֲדָשׁוֹת מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל, וְעַל פִּיהֶם נִתְחַדֵּשׁ גַּם כֵּן עִנְיָנִים בָּעוֹלָם. וּמִמַּצַּב הָעוֹלָם בְּכָל דּוֹר נוּכַל לְהִתְבּוֹנֵן עַל מַצַּב נַפְשׁוֹת יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁבַּדּוֹר, וְכֵן עַל מַצַּב הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּפִיּוֹת תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים הָאֲמִתִּיִּים שֶׁבְּאוֹתוֹ דּוֹר וּלְכָךְ אָמְרוּ בְּחֲגִיגָה (ה:): "אָבְדָה עֵצָה מִבָּנִים – נִסְרְחָה חָכְמָתָם", עַיֵּין שָׁם וּמוּבָן]:
records.originEnglish: And just as souls change from generation to generation, so does the Torah—namely the Oral Torah wherein new insights are revealed in every generation by the sages of Israel; and through each novel revelation of the Oral Torah, new souls emerge into the light, and through them worldly events and circumstances are likewise transformed. And from the geopolitical condition of the world in every era, we can discern the spiritual stature of the souls of Israel in that generation, and likewise the status of the Torah residing in the mouths of authentic scholars in that era and therefore they stated in Chagigah 5b: "If counsel is lost from the children, their wisdom becomes corrupted," see there, and it is understood.

records.themeTitle: Returning the power received through a possession
records.themeSummary: The material means of livelihood carries life from its divine source.
records.explanation: Tiferet Yosef explains what returning a possession to its source can mean while a person still uses it. Food is a garment through which life is received; the error is to treat that garment as an independent giver of life. The omer models receiving and returning the power in recognition of its Giver. This develops the siman’s account of livelihood as a place where one’s life is lodged, rather than reducing the connection to ownership alone.
records.targetEnglish: The order of these teachings has this meaning. As my grandfather, of blessed memory, said: whenever a person gives an acquisition over to Hashem, Hashem gives that acquisition back to the person with greater strength. Thus, ‘Bring an omer before Me on Pesach’: in this world Hashem placed garments from which a person receives the strength of his life. In truth, the principal life-giving power is the utterance of Hashem’s mouth contained in that garment. If a person takes the garment without recognizing that this utterance is primary, imagining instead that the garment gives him life, he not only fails to receive the utterance; the garment conceals it from him still further. Hashem therefore counsels us to take more than the garment itself, always recognizing the utterance within it. ‘Bring an omer before Me on Pesach’ teaches that at the very beginning of receiving a benefit, when its inward meaning is not yet recognized, it is still called animal food. A benefit whose inward meaning a person does not recognize is animal food. He should return that power to Hashem; this is what the omer offering signifies. Hashem promises that the grain in the fields will be blessed: He will give the person recognition of the benefit, so that he recognizes its inward meaning. This is called the grain in the fields—human food.
records.originHebrew: וְהַמֵּבִין עַל דָּבָר יוּכַל לָדַעַת וּלְהִתְבּוֹנֵן לְתַקֵּן כָּל אֵלֶּה, וְהַתִּיקּוּן הוּא רַק עַל יְדֵי הַהֲשָׁבָה לַמָּקוֹר שֶׁיֵּדַע שֶׁהַכֹּל הוּא מֵעֶצֶם חַיּוּת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁמְּחַיֵּיהוּ וּמְקַיְּימוֹ, זוּלַת זֶה הָיוּ כְּלֹא הָיָה
records.originEnglish: And he who discerns these matters can understand and reflect on how to rectify all of them, and this rectification is achieved solely by returning them to the Source: recognizing that everything exists exclusively through the essential vitality of the Blessed Name Who animates and preserves it, without which it would vanish into nothingness
records.targetHebrew: ענין של הסדר הזה, כמו שאמר אזמו"ר זללה"ה שבכל קנין שאדם מוסר להשי"ת, מוסר השי"ת אותו הקנין בחזרה אל האדם ביתר שאת. וזה הביאו לפני עומר בפסח,כי בעוה"ז הציב השי"ת לבושים אשר האדם נוטל מהם כח חיותו. ובאמת עיקר כח המחיה הוא המוצא פי ד' המונח בהלבוש הזה. ובאם האדם יקח את הלבוש, ולא יכיר שעיקר הוא המוצא פי ד', ורק ידמה לו שהלבוש הוא המחיה אותו, לא די שאינו נוטל המוצא פי ד', רק שהלבוש יסתיר אותו ביותר. וזה שנותן לנו השי"ת עצה, שבל יקח את הלבוש בעצמו, רק יכיר תמיד המוצא פי ד' המונח בהלבוש. וזה, הביאו לפני עומר בפסח, זה מורה שתיכף בעת התחלת קבלת הטובה, שאז אינו מכיר הפנימיות מהטובה, ונקרא אז עדיין מאכל בהמה. כי בטובה כזאת שאדם אינו מכיר הפנימיות מהטובה הוא מאכל בהמה, ויחזיר זה הכח להשי"ת, וזה מורה קרבן עומר. ומבטיח לו השי"ת, שיתברך תבואה שבשדות. היינו שיתן לאדם הכרה בהטובה שיכיר הפנימיות מהטובה. וזה נקרא תבואה שבשדות, היינו מאכל אדם.

records.targetRef: Sod Yesharim, The First Night of Pesach 1:1
records.themeTitle: Gifted clarity and lasting acquisition
records.themeSummary: Understanding granted without effort still calls for a response that makes it enduring.
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim distinguishes the intensity of a revelation from its permanence. A person may grasp something through an extraordinary gift and still lose it; work makes the understanding fixed in the heart. This clarifies why Rav Tzadok treats the Flood generation’s taste of the world to come as an opening to repentance whose purpose was not fulfilled merely by experiencing it.
records.targetEnglish: Here, however, the expanded state came first. As the writings of the holy Ari teach, on this night the expanded consciousness preceded the constricted consciousness. The expanded state is like someone who understands a matter because he has a great intellect, without any labor at all. Yet, because it came without labor, he can easily forget it. This is unlike someone who understood a matter through labor: it becomes fixed in his heart so that he cannot forget it. Although this is called the constricted state, the matter is nevertheless fixed in his heart like a peg that will not move.
records.originHebrew: [צב] לִפְעָמִים נִפְתָּח לָאָדָם מַדְרֵגוֹת, וְאִם הוּא רַק לְפִי שָׁעָה וְאַחַר כָּךְ נֶעְלָם מִמֶּנּוּ וְהוּא חוֹזֵר לְסוּרוֹ לִהְיוֹת מְשׁוּקָּע בַּתַּאֲווֹת – יֵשׁ לוֹ לְהִתְבּוֹנֵן וְלִדְאוֹג פֶּן הוּא חַס וְשָׁלוֹם עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּפֶרֶק חֵלֶק (סַנְהֶדְרִין קח:) בְּדוֹר הַמַּבּוּל, שֶׁהִטְעִימָן מֵעֵין עוֹלָם הַבָּא; וַהֲרֵי אָמְרוּ בְּפֶרֶק הָיָה קוֹרֵא שֶׁהָעוֹלָם הַבָּא אֵין בּוֹ שׁוּם הֲנָאָה וְחֶמְדָּה מֵעִנְיְנֵי תַּאֲווֹת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה, רַק נֶהֱנִין מִזִּיו הַשְּׁכִינָה, וְאַחַר פְּתִיחַת אוֹר כָּזֶה הֲרֵי לֹא הָיוּ עוֹד בְּנֵי מַבּוּל, רַק עַל כָּרְחֲךָ שֶׁנִּפְתַּח לָהֶם לְשָׁעָה וְנֶעְלַם; וְהוּא אֶחָד עִם הַדָּבָר אַחֵר דְּשָׁם דְּקָאָמַר: "זְמַן קָטָן אַחַר זְמַן גָּדוֹל", שֶׁזֶּה הָיָה זְמַן אוּלַי יָשׁוּבוּ עַל יְדֵי זֶה שֶׁפָּתַח לָהֶם הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ אוֹר כָּזֶה, שֶׁהוּא גַּם כֵּן הֶעְדֵּר הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע, וְאַחַר כָּךְ הֶעֱלִימוֹ כְּרֶגַע וְחָזְרוּ לְתַאֲוָתָם.
records.originEnglish: Sometimes spiritual levels are opened unto a person, and if it is only temporary and afterward vanishes from him so that he returns to his waywardness, becoming immersed in desires—he must reflect and worry lest he be, Heaven forbid, in the category of what our Sages said in chapter Chelek (Sanhedrin 108a) regarding the Generation of the Flood, that He gave them a foretaste of the World to Come; and behold, they said in the chapter Hayah Koreh (Berakhot 17a) that the World to Come contains no pleasure or lust of worldly matters, but only delighting in the radiance of the Shechinah, and after the opening of such an illumination they should no longer have been corrupt, so perforce it opened to them for a brief hour and then vanished; and this is synonymous with the alternative interpretation there that says: "a short time after a long time," meaning an interval wherein perhaps they would repent through the Blessed Name opening such light to them—which also removes the evil inclination—and afterward He concealed it in an instant and they returned to their lust.

records.themeTitle: What remains after Torah study
records.themeSummary: The lasting effect of study is distinguished from drawing Torah into the heart at the outset.
records.explanation: The Ishbitz teaching defines permanence by what remains after the act of learning. That distinction illuminates the siman’s opening difficulty: receiving light does not yet make it a fixed possession. The comparison supplements the existing historical explanation of the Second Temple with a description of the inward result sought by the learner.
records.targetEnglish: The meaning of a blessing after it is what remains permanently in a person’s heart after he engages in Torah. A blessing before it concerns the person’s drawing words of Torah into his heart. But the result of those words of Torah that he has drawn into himself should remain in his heart permanently, like a peg that will never move. That permanence is called the blessing after it.
records.originHebrew: [צג] תְּחִלָּה הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מֵאִיר לָאָדָם, וְהָאָדָם אֵין רָגִיל בָּזֶה עֲדַיִן וְקָשֶׁה עָלָיו לְקַבְּלוֹ כְּיָתֵד קָבוּעַ בְּמָקוֹם נֶאֱמָן שֶׁלֹּא יִמּוֹט, וּמְאַבְּדוֹ; וְאַחַר כָּךְ הָאָדָם נוֹהֶה אַחֲרָיו וּמְבַקְּשׁוֹ, וְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ אֵינוֹ חוֹזֵר וּפוֹתֵחַ לוֹ, כְּטַעֲנַת "הֲשִׁיבֵנוּ וְכוּלֵי", אִם לֹא בְּקֹשִׁי גָּדוֹל, כְּעִנְיַן "כְּשֶׁרָצִיתִי לֹא רָצִיתָ, עַכְשָׁו וְכוּלֵי" (בְּרָכוֹת ז.).
records.originEnglish: Initially, the Blessed Name illuminates a person, but the person is not yet accustomed to this and finds it difficult to secure it as a nail driven into a firm place so that it will not give way, and he loses it; and afterward the person yearns after Him and seeks Him, but the Blessed Name does not readily reopen it to him, parallel to the plea of "Bring us back, etc.," unless with great difficulty, in the manner of: "When I desired, you did not desire; now, etc." (Berakhot 7a).

records.themeTitle: The passage from awe to love
records.themeSummary: An awakening of fear can become a stage in a fuller return.
records.explanation: Resisei Layla describes the movement that the siman compresses into a few lines: self-concern gives way to awe before Hashem, and awe can lead to love. The quoted sequence explains why the first alarming illumination is an opening that requires a response, rather than a condition in which the person is meant to remain.
records.targetEnglish: These three kinds of repentance proceed from below upward. First a person has compassion on himself; this is easy for anyone to awaken on his own. Afterward he begins to feel awe before Hashem and the splendor of His majesty, and through this he sighs over his sins. Afterward he comes to love of Hashem and weeps before Him over what has already passed and is no longer.
records.originHebrew: צד] פְּעָמִים מַשִּׂיג הָאָדָם הֶאָרָה, וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה מַגִּיעַ לְיִרְאָה, וְהוּא פָּנִים שֶׁל זַעַם; וּכְשֶׁמַּגִּיעַ עַל יָדוֹ לְאַהֲבָה, הוּא פָּנִים שֶׁל רָצוֹן; וְעַל יְדֵי הַיִּרְאָה שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ, הוּא מְתַקֵּן הַזַּעַם שֶׁבַּפָּנִים וּמִתְהַפֵּךְ לְרָצוֹן, וּבָא אַחַר כָּךְ לְאַהֲבָה.
records.originEnglish: Sometimes a person attains an illumination, and through it reaches awe/fear, which is the aspect of a severe, wrathful countenance (panim shel za'am); and when through it he ascends to love, it is a countenance of favor (panim shel ratzon); and through the awe he possesses, he rectifies the wrath of the countenance, transforming it into favor, subsequently arriving at love.

records.targetRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Noach 5
records.themeTitle: The luminous rainbow as visible assurance
records.themeSummary: The promise becomes recognizable even amid fear and concealment.
records.explanation: Mei HaShiloach reads the cloud as concealment and the rainbow as the strength to trust within it. Its explanation of the rainbow’s luminous colors therefore clarifies the siman’s closing point: messianic illumination makes the assurance of the covenant apparent. The source’s contrast between occasional and constant perception also explains why the language concerns a revealed sign rather than confidence inferred from outward calm.
records.targetEnglish: ‘When I bring a cloud over the earth, the rainbow will appear in the cloud.’ A cloud means awe and concealment; a rainbow means strong confidence. Even amid the intensity of awe you will have great trust. This is what the Holy One promised Noach. Thus the holy Zohar says (Bereshit 72b): do not anticipate the footsteps of Mashiach until you see a rainbow in luminous colors. This means: when the assurance from Hashem is clear and explicit before your eyes, then anticipate the footsteps of Mashiach. This is why Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai asked Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi (Ketubot 77b), ‘Was the rainbow seen in your days?’ He did not ask, ‘Did you see it?’ ‘Was seen’ implies sometimes, rather than constantly; for Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai the rainbow was constant. Israel’s rainbow and strength are the passage of Shema Yisrael, which gives strength to the hearts of those who hope for His kindness.
records.originHebrew: וְזֶה שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר נֹחַ (עב עַמּוּד ב) וּבַתִּיקּוּנִים (תִּיקּוּן יח): "כַּד תֶּחֱמֵי קַשְׁתָּא בְּאַנְפִּין נְהִירִין תְּצַפֵּי לְרַגְלֵי מְשִׁיחָא", שֶׁהַקֶּשֶׁת הוּא אוֹת הַבְּרִית נֶגֶד עוֹנְשֵׁי חַטֹּאת נְעוּרִים, וּבְדוֹרוֹ שֶׁל מָשִׁיחַ יִהְיֶה זֶה בְּאַנְפִּין נְהִירִין בְּהֶאָרַת פָּנִים, שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מֵאִיר עֵינֵיהֶם לָדַעַת כִּי סָר עֲוֹנָם בָּזֶה, וְ"עַמֵּךְ כֻּלָּם צַדִּיקִים וְגוֹמֵר", פֵּירוּשׁ שׁוֹמְרֵי הַבְּרִית כַּנּוֹדָע:
records.originEnglish: And this is what is stated in the Zohar (Noach 72b) and in the Tikkunim (Tikkun 18): "When you see the rainbow in radiant hues, anticipate the footsteps of the Messiah," for the rainbow is the sign of the Covenant counter to the retributions of the sins of youth, and in the generation of the Messiah this will appear in radiant hues with a luminous countenance, where the Blessed Name enlightens their eyes to know that their iniquity has departed in this realm, and "your people are all righteous, etc." (Isaiah 60:21), meaning guardians of the Covenant, as is known.
records.targetHebrew: וְהָיָה בְּעַנְנִי עָנָן עַל הָאָרֶץ וְנִרְאֲתָה הַקֶּשֶׁת בֶּעָנָן. עָנָן הַיְינוּ יִרְאָה וְהֶסְתֵּר, וְקֶשֶׁת הַיְינוּ מִבְטַח עוֹז, כִּי בְּכׇל תֹּקֶף הַיִּרְאָה יִהְיֶה לְךָ בִּטָּחוֹן גָּדוֹל וְזֹאת הִבְטִיחַ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לְנֹחַ. וְזֶה שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר בַּזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ (בְּרֵאשִׁית עב:): לָא תְצַפֵּי לְרַגְלֵי דִמְשִׁיחָא עַד דְּתִחְזֵי קַשְׁתָּא בִּגְוָנִין נְהוֹרִין, הַיְינוּ שֶׁיִּהְיוּ הַתַּקִּיפוּת מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בּוֹלֵט וּמְפוֹרָשׁ נֶגֶד עֵינֶיךָ, אָז תְּצַפֶּה לְרַגְלֵי דִמְשִׁיחָא. וְזֶה שֶׁשָּׁאַל רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַאי אֶת רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי (כְּתוּבּוֹת עז:): "נִרְאֲתָה הַקֶּשֶׁת בְּיָמֶיךָ?", וְלֹא שָׁאַל אוֹתוֹ בִּלְשׁוֹן "רָאִיתָ", דְּ"נִרְאֲתָה" מַשְׁמַע לִפְעָמִים וְלֹא בִּתְמִידוּת, וּלְרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַאי הָיְתָה הַקֶּשֶׁת בִּתְמִידוּת. וְהַקֶּשֶׁת וְהַתַּקִּיפוּת שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל הוּא פָּרָשַׁת שְׁמַע יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁהוּא נוֹתֵן תַּקִּיפוּת בְּלֵב הַמְיַחֲלִים לְחַסְדּוֹ.

records.themeTitle: A rooted covenant revealed through action
records.themeSummary: Intrinsic covenantal holiness and the commanded act are both retained.
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim develops the same vow-law proof while preserving a crucial qualification. Israel’s rooted relation to the covenant is not created by the physical act, yet the act remains necessary to disclose it. This helps explain the siman’s distinction between an outwardly unblemished appearance and belonging at the root of the covenant, without making the final assurance a reason to disregard the mitzvah.
records.targetEnglish: ‘Gladness’ is circumcision, as it says, ‘I rejoice over Your utterance.’ Here too the matter is of this kind. Circumcision appears to a person as though he is repairing a lack that Hashem created in him. Yet did Hashem, Heaven forbid, create a lack? In truth, the holiness of circumcision is completely fixed in every soul of Israel even before he circumcises himself. As the Gemara says (Nedarim 31b): one who vows not to benefit from the uncircumcised may benefit from uncircumcised Israelites but may not benefit from circumcised gentiles; one who vows not to benefit from the circumcised may not benefit from uncircumcised Israelites but may benefit from circumcised gentiles. Uncircumcision is named only after the latter, as it says, ‘For all the nations are uncircumcised.’ Thus gentiles are called uncircumcised even when circumcised, and an Israelite is called circumcised even while uncircumcised. This proves that the holiness of circumcision is fixed and enduring in Israel even without their act of service. Yet a person cannot recognize that permanently present holiness except by first circumcising himself. Every person must therefore initially experience concealment, imagining that Hashem created a lack in him and that he repairs it through his service. Through this concealment every soul is obliged to circumcise himself. After he is circumcised, it is revealed retrospectively that the holiness of circumcision is permanently within him.
records.originHebrew: כִּי קַיְימָא לַן בִּנְדָרִים (לא:): הַנּוֹדֵר מִן הָעֲרֵלִים אָסוּר בְּמוּלֵי אֻמּוֹת עוֹבְדֵי כּוֹכָבִים וּמוּתָּר בְּעַרְלֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל, שֶׁאֵין הָעָרְלָה נִקְרָא אֶלָּא עַל שְׁמָם, אֲפִילּוּ הֵם מוּלִים וְשׁוֹמְרֵי הַבְּרִית. וְ"עַמֵּךְ כֻּלָּם צַדִּיקִים" וְשׁוֹמְרֵי הַבְּרִית, אֲפִילּוּ שֶׁקִּלְקְלוּ:

And "your people are all righteous" and guardians of the Covenant, even when they have stumbled.

records.targetRef: Tiferet Yosef, Talmud Anthology, Rosh Hashanah 1
records.themeTitle: A closed route of atonement and the possibility of repair
records.themeSummary: The exclusion of offerings does not exclude Torah and acts of kindness.
records.explanation: Tiferet Yosef spells out the inference Rav Tzadok invokes. The added words about sacrifice in the prophecy concerning Eli’s house identify a limit on one means of atonement while opening another. This is the logical comparison behind the siman’s reading of the Zohar’s severe language; it does not erase the need for the actual repair described by the source.
records.targetEnglish: Rava said: through sacrifice and meal offering it is not atoned, but it is atoned through Torah. Abaye said: it is atoned through Torah and acts of kindness. Thus the Talmud says (Megillah 31b) that on Rosh Hashanah we read ‘Hashem remembered Sarah’ and take the haftarah from Channah. Earlier it is written (I Samuel 2:27), ‘A man of God came to Eli,’ continuing through ‘all the increase of your house.’ The Sifrei identifies this man as Elkanah, Shmuel’s father. What did Shmuel add in his prophecy, when his father had already delivered that prophecy? He added its concluding words: ‘Whether the sin of Eli’s house shall be atoned through sacrifice and meal offering.’ The inference is: through sacrifice and meal offering it is not atoned, but it is atoned through Torah and acts of kindness. Even a decree accompanied by an oath therefore has a repair. Elkanah’s earlier prophecy had supplied no repair; Shmuel added that there is nothing in the world for which there is no repair. This is why we take the haftarah from Channah: even a decree accompanied by an oath has a repair.
records.originHebrew: וּבַזֹּהַר בְּרֵאשִׁית וְנֹחַ: דְּלֵית מְסָאָבָא כְּמוֹהוּ. וְהִנֵּה אָמְרוּ בְּפֶרֶק ב דִּבְרָכוֹת (טז.) דְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה מַעֲלִין מִטֻּמְאָה לְטָהֳרָה. וּמַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר נֹחַ (סב עַמּוּד א) דְּאֵין מוֹעִיל תְּשׁוּבָה, הוּא עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה יח.): בְּזֶבַח אֵין מִתְכַּפֵּר, אֲבָל מִתְכַּפֵּר בַּתּוֹרָה; הָכָא נַמֵּי כֵּן; וּכְמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה שִׁילְהֵי חֲגִיגָה: תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים אֵין אוֹר שֶׁל גֵּיהִנָּם שׁוֹלֵט בָּהֶם.
records.originEnglish: And in the Zohar (Bereishit and Noach): there is no defilement like it. And behold, they said in the second chapter of Berakhot (16a) that words of Torah elevate from impurity to purity. And what is written in Zohar Noach (62a) that repentance does not avail, is along the lines of Rosh Hashanah 18a: through sacrifice it is not atoned, but it is atoned through Torah; here too it is so; and as our Sages expounded at the end of Chagigah (27a): the fire of Gehenna has no dominion over Torah scholars.

records.themeTitle: The letters that record a miracle and the power they carry
records.themeSummary: The Torah account participates in the life of the matter it describes.
records.explanation: Poked Akarim provides Rav Tzadok’s fuller formulation of the siman’s opening principle. The correspondence is more than a useful reminder: the letters recording the event are described as Torah through which its power is drawn. The distinction between written and Oral Torah also keeps the account from being reduced to a single technique involving written divine names.
records.targetEnglish: All Israel’s miracles and deliverances are through the power of Torah. Miracles in Scripture are through the power of the very letters in which the miracle is written; those are the substance of Torah through which the miracle is drawn. This is also known concerning the operation of divine names: in the letters of the verse describing a miracle is alluded the name that effects that matter. As the Tikkunim say (Tikkun 69), the name ‘Hakhtav’ comes from the verse ‘The writing was the writing of God’ (Exodus 32:16), and ‘Hadoresh’ from ‘To know how to sustain the weary with a word’ (Isaiah 50:4), and similarly elsewhere. It is so at the plain level too, through the power of those words of Torah. Every word of Torah has pardes—plain meaning, allusion, exposition, and secret—as is known; through these four ways, too, those words of Torah have the power to effect the miracle. Miracles that were not given to be written occur through the power of Oral Torah. This began after the miracle of Esther.

records.themeTitle: Remembering one’s task while Hashem puts the sin aside
records.themeSummary: The final instruction preserves personal responsibility within the promise of forgiveness.
records.explanation: Beit Yaakov explicitly places the two directions together: the person keeps the sin before him, while Hashem puts it aside. This comparison helps read the siman’s final sentence alongside its description of completed forgiveness. Rav Tzadok describes the peace of complete repair, while the person’s chosen task remains honest remembrance and return; ordinary loss of memory is not itself the spiritual attainment described here.
records.targetEnglish: Conversely, if a person remembers his sin and fulfills ‘My sin is always before me’ (Psalms 51:5), then Hashem makes Himself forgetful and does not look at that sin at all.

records.themeTitle: Why the returning sinner is called Hashem’s chasid
records.themeSummary: The designation follows a stronger conquest of the inclination through real return.
records.explanation: Takanat HaShavin explains the same possessive expression through the returning sinner’s greater effort. Its context distinguishes a moment of sincere return from repentance that has become a settled identity. Read beside the siman, this keeps ‘Your pious ones’ tied to actual transformation after repentance, rather than treating the old sin as meritorious while it remains unrepaired.
records.targetEnglish: Therefore they said in the Letters of Rabbi Akiva concerning the verse ‘Your pious ones shall sing’: these are the sinners of Israel who are destined to return. A sinner needs greater force of strength in conquering the inclination when he returns; therefore he is called ‘Your pious ones,’ meaning Hashem’s pious ones—those of exceptional piety. It is like ‘the trees of Hashem’ and ‘the cedars of Hashem’: wherever something is joined to Hashem’s name, it indicates its exceptional degree. Someone before whom an occasion for sin comes and who escapes it is called ‘mighty in strength’ (Kiddushin 40a). Through this he is assured of being guarded from then on, until he acquires through it the fixed name of a baal teshuvah.
